design_detail: Open within-person comparison of five racemic ketamine preparations in three healthy Japanese men. Each man received all five, at least one week apart: a 20 mg intravenous injection of a commercial preparation given over 15 seconds; two tablets containing 25 mg each, taken with 100 mL of water; two sublingual tablets containing 25 mg each, placed under the tongue; one suppository containing 50 mg; and a nasal spray of an aqueous solution containing 25 mg, applied to the nasal mucous membrane with an atomizer. The tablet and the suppository were preparations made by the authors' own group. Blood was taken before dosing and at thirteen times over 8 hours, and the (R)- and (S)-enantiomers of ketamine and of its metabolite norketamine were measured by stereoselective high-performance liquid chromatography with ultraviolet detection. The intravenous data were fitted biexponentially; bioavailability of each other preparation was the dose-adjusted ratio of its area to the same people's intravenous area. There was no placebo, no stated randomization or order, no blinding, and no pain, sedation or adverse-effect measure of any kind.
can_establish: The plasma concentration-time course of each enantiomer of ketamine and of norketamine over 8 hours after each of five racemic preparations in three healthy men, and the systemic availability of the four non-injected preparations relative to the same men's intravenous curves.
cannot_establish: Anything about pain relief, sedation, dissociation or adverse effects, since nothing was measured besides plasma concentrations; any difference or equivalence between preparations or between enantiomers (three people, no test statistics printed); the behaviour of these preparations in patients with pain, in women, or in anyone with ketamine experience; the duration of exposure by any route other than intravenous, for which alone a half-life is reported; and the precision of any parameter, since no detection limit, no interval and no individual values are given.

sample.recruitment: Three healthy male volunteers who gave informed consent; how they were identified or approached is not stated. The protocol was approved by the hospital's ethics committee (p. 38).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated beyond being healthy. No medical screening, medication, tobacco, caffeine or drug history is reported. Alcohol was not permitted for 24 hours before and during the study (p. 38).
sample.demographics: Three men, aged 27-40 years and weighing 60-72 kg. No individual values, no further characteristics and no data on health, smoking or medication are given (p. 38).
sample.attrition: Not reported; the tables state that every value is a mean with standard deviation, and the figure legend says each point is the mean of three determinations.
sample.selection_effects: Three healthy men from an unstated source. No woman, no patient and nobody with ketamine experience took part, and the preparations were being developed for people with neuropathic pain, in whom absorption, metabolism and the amount of drug reaching the circulation may all differ. With three people, each man contributes a third of every mean, so a single unusual absorption (the authors note that not everyone had a rectal enema before the suppository) moves the published figure for a whole route.

exposure.measurement: Drug given and measured in the laboratory. (R)- and (S)-ketamine and (R)- and (S)-norketamine in plasma by stereoselective high-performance liquid chromatography after three successive liquid-liquid extractions, with a chiral column at 35 degrees C, a hexane and 2-propanol mobile phase at 0.8 mL/min and ultraviolet detection at 215 nm; the four retention times are given as 11.6, 13.5, 25 and 27 minutes and no interfering peaks were seen. No limit of quantification, calibration range, precision or accuracy is reported, although several conclusions rest on values described as below the detection limit (pp. 38-39).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, each separated by at least one week: a single intravenous injection of 20 mg given over 15 seconds, from a commercial 10 mg/mL preparation; two tablets of 25 mg each taken with 100 mL of water; two sublingual tablets of 25 mg each placed under the tongue; one 50 mg suppository in a fatty base; and an aqueous solution containing 25 mg given as a nasal spray with an atomizer. All preparations were racemic. Blood (about 6 mL each time) was taken before dosing and at 5, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 minutes and at 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 hours (p. 38).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. No other drug, tobacco or caffeine use is reported and none was screened for; alcohol was prohibited for 24 hours before and during the study (p. 38).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least one week between preparations, and no alcohol for 24 hours before and during the study. Whether participants were fasting is not stated, which matters for the tablet and the sublingual tablet (p. 38).

comparison.controls: Within-person only: each man's own intravenous curve is the reference against which the other four preparations are measured. There is no placebo, no untreated session and no comparison group.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover in which all three men received all five preparations, but no randomization, counterbalancing or order of the five sessions is described, so any change over the five weeks or more of the study cannot be separated from the preparation.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the pharmacokinetic questions; the only pre-dose measurement is the blank plasma sample, whose values are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma concentration-time curves for each enantiomer of ketamine and norketamine. The intravenous curves were fitted to a biexponential equation with a nonlinear least-squares program to obtain the intercepts and rate constants, from which the area under the curve, total body clearance and the steady-state volume of distribution were derived; areas after the other four preparations were obtained by the trapezoidal rule and extrapolated to infinity, and norketamine areas by the trapezoidal rule to 8 hours; bioavailability was the dose-adjusted ratio of a preparation's area to the intravenous area (pp. 38-39). No pharmacodynamic instrument of any kind was used.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable: no clinical or behavioural measure was taken. The assay is cited to the authors' own earlier chromatographic paper and no validation data are reproduced here.
outcomes.operationalization: Usefulness for neuropathic pain is inferred entirely from plasma concentrations and bioavailability, by analogy with earlier reports that ketamine and norketamine have analgesic properties. No pain, sedation, dissociation or adverse-effect outcome was recorded, so nothing in this study is operationalized as either benefit or harm.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The only analysis named is an analysis of variance with 0.05 as the minimal level of significance (p. 39). Ten pharmacokinetic parameters are reported for two enantiomers across five preparations, seventy tabulated values in all, and the paper states that nothing differed significantly between enantiomers or between preparations without printing a single test statistic, degree of freedom or p value (pp. 40-42).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None. The study was open: participants and investigators knew which preparation was being given at every session, and no blinding, masking or dummy is mentioned anywhere. For a plasma-concentration outcome this matters less than it would for a rated outcome, but it bears on the handling of the sublingual condition, in which participants swallowed saliva.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means with standard deviations only; no confidence intervals, no individual values and no standardized effect sizes. Intravenous 20 mg, (R)- and (S)-ketamine: terminal half-life 126.8 min (SD 47.4) and 117.3 (47.9); area to infinity 138.0 ng*h/mL (15.6) and 126.3 (15.1); total clearance 1.1 L/h/kg (0.2) and 1.2 (0.1); steady-state volume of distribution 2.5 L/kg (0.6) and 2.5 (0.8). Peak concentration, time to peak, area and bioavailability for the other preparations, (R)- then (S)-: tablet 50 mg, 42.6 ng/mL (13.3) and 40.4 (14.2), 33.3 min (15.3) and 30.0 (30.0), 72.3 (22.4) and 64.9 (27.4), 18.3% (4.7) and 17.6% (3.8); sublingual tablet 50 mg, 61.6 (21.3) and 56.9 (22.8), 40.0 (20.0) and 36.7 (20.8), 108.8 (17.3) and 110.5 (18.4), 32.2% (8.2) and 32.1% (7.2); suppository 50 mg, 42.8 (31.1) and 38.8 (30.2), 23.3 (5.7) and 23.3 (5.7), 102.4 (76.7) and 87.9 (78.9), 28.9% (18.9) and 30.8% (30.6); nasal spray 25 mg, 29.4 (16.5) and 29.3 (13.8), 22.5 (9.6) and 17.5 (5.0), 76.8 (27.9) and 72.7 (17.5), 43.8% (11.4) and 46.4% (12.9) (Table 1, p. 41). Norketamine peak, time to peak and area to 8 hours, (R)- then (S)-: injection 38.1 ng/mL (6.1) and 34.9 (6.4), 23.3 min (5.8) both, 173.8 ng*h/mL (26.5) and 149.8 (9.5); tablet 188.1 (4.7) and 172.0 (13.7), 50.0 (17.3) both, 533.8 (47.1) and 494.9 (73.0); sublingual 123.4 (10.7) and 109.7 (16.6), 113.3 (70.2) and 93.3 (75.7), 462.9 (65.2) and 408.7 (35.1); suppository 85.3 (35.1) and 78.7 (30.9), 33.3 (15.3) both, 322.6 (106.5) and 282.6 (74.2); nasal spray 33.1 (25.3) and 29.4 (21.3), 120.0 (52.0) and 100.0 (17.3), 115.9 (17.6) and 100.7 (39.6) (Table 2, p. 42). Editors' calculations from these tables: the norketamine-to-ketamine area ratio is 7.4 for the (R)- and 7.6 for the (S)-enantiomer after the tablet, 4.3 and 3.7 after the sublingual tablet, 3.2 and 3.2 after the suppository, and 1.5 and 1.4 after the nasal spray; recomputing bioavailability from the tabulated mean areas rather than from individual ratios gives 21.0% and 20.6% for the tablet, 31.5% and 35.0% for the sublingual tablet, 29.7% and 27.8% for the suppository and 44.5% and 46.0% for the nasal spray.
analysis.covariates: None; means of three people, with no adjustment and no modelling of person as a factor beyond the unreported analysis of variance.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. Ethics-committee approval and informed consent are stated (p. 38).
analysis.selective_reporting: A terminal half-life is printed only for the intravenous injection; none is given for the tablet, sublingual tablet, suppository or nasal spray, so how long ketamine persists after those preparations cannot be read from this paper. No test statistic or p value is printed for any of the stated null comparisons. Two preliminary sub-studies appear only in the Discussion, with no methods and no data: a comparison of the sublingual tablet with and without swallowing saliva for one hour, said to lower the one-hour area and peak concentration by 35-50%, with the number of participants not stated; and a two-amount comparison of the nasal spray in a single volunteer, said to show an almost linear increase in area (pp. 42-43).
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With three people the standard deviations approach or exceed the means for several parameters, for example the suppository's bioavailability, 28.9% (SD 18.9) for the (R)- and 30.8% (SD 30.6) for the (S)-enantiomer, and its area, 102.4 (SD 76.7) and 87.9 (SD 78.9) ng*h/mL. A statement that preparations did not differ significantly, drawn from data like these, carries almost no information about whether they differ.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In three healthy men, plasma ketamine fell biexponentially after an intravenous injection with a terminal half-life of about two hours for both enantiomers. Relative to that reference, about 18% of a swallowed tablet, about 32% of a sublingual tablet, about 29-31% of a suppository and about 44-46% of a nasal spray reached the circulation. Norketamine exposure was greatest after the tablet (about seven and a half times the ketamine area) and least after the nasal spray (about one and a half times), which the authors read as first-pass metabolism being avoided to different degrees by the different routes. The two enantiomers behaved alike in these three men.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the conclusion state that these pharmacokinetic findings suggest all the preparations tested may be useful for the alleviation of neuropathic pain, and propose that the type of preparation should be chosen according to the patient's condition and the amount of ketamine required; the Discussion adds specific clinical recommendations about who should receive which preparation. No patient took part, and no pain or any other effect was measured, so every statement about usefulness is an inference from plasma concentrations plus the authors' own earlier tablet study and animal work. The statement that parameters did not differ between the enantiomers or between the preparations is a null result in three people, reported with no test statistics, and is presented in the Discussion as a finding to be contrasted with an earlier study that did find enantiomer differences, with the difference attributed to ethnicity.

timeline.event: Oral bioavailability of ketamine about 17% and intramuscular about 93% in healthy volunteers, computed against an intravenous reference in four people per route

Stereoselective study in surgical patients (Geisslinger et al.) found lower clearance and volume of distribution for the (R)- than the (S)-enantiomer, which this study did not reproduce; its authors attribute the difference to ethnicity

Ketamine and norketamine concentrations after intravenous, nasal and rectal administration in children (Malinovsky et al.), with nasal and rectal bioavailability of about 50% and 25%, cited here as the closest comparison

Three-way crossover of a sublingual and oral formulation in six people with neuropathic pain (Chong et al.), which reported a later time to peak after swallowing than after sublingual dosing, the reverse of the ordering found here
Clinical pharmacokinetics review tabulates every row of this study and carries its figures forward as the bioavailability of ketamine by the rectal (about 30%) and nasal (about 45%) routes

replication.where_it_stands: This three-person study is the only source read here for the systemic availability of sublingual, rectal and nasal racemic ketamine in adults, and it is the study the 2016 clinical review cites for the rectal and nasal figures that circulate in the literature. Its oral figure agrees with the 1982 four-person estimate. None of the four non-injected figures has been re-measured in a larger adult sample in the sources read here, and the sublingual condition as performed here was partly gastrointestinal, since participants swallowed saliva.

funding.funder: Not reported: the paper carries no funding statement (pp. 37-43).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: there is no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Pharmacy, Faculty of Medicine, The University of Tokyo Hospital, and the departments of hospital pharmacy and anaesthesiology of a Tokyo hospital. The tablet and the suppository tested were made by the authors' own group, and the authors' earlier paper on preparing ketamine tablets, and their earlier paper on the assay, are cited as the basis for both. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, order-balanced crossover with enough participants for interval estimates, in both sexes and in the patients for whom these preparations are intended, with an assay of stated sensitivity and precision, an elimination half-life reported for every route, sublingual dosing performed with swallowing controlled and verified, and a pre-specified clinical outcome (pain and adverse effects) measured alongside the plasma concentrations.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the five preparations)
domains.note: No randomization, counterbalancing, allocation or order of the five sessions is described. With three people and five sessions spread over at least five weeks, order and period effects cannot be separated from the preparation.

At least a week between preparations, far longer than the measured terminal half-life of about two hours, and concentrations were below the detection limit by 4-8 hours; but pre-dose concentrations are never reported, the detection limit is never stated, and the order of sessions is unknown.

domains.domain: Deviations from intended interventions (blinding and delivery)
domains.note: Open administration with no placebo. Two conditions departed from their labels: the Discussion states that participants swallowed the sublingual tablets using saliva, so that condition includes gastrointestinal absorption, and that not all participants had a rectal enema before the suppository, which the authors give as the reason for the large variation in the rectal values. The amount delivered by the atomizer is acknowledged to be hard to control.

No missing data are declared, but no half-life is reported for four of the five preparations, and several times to peak cannot be reconciled with three observations at the stated sampling times (see reporting issues), which suggests the tables do not rest on exactly three values throughout.

A stereoselective chromatographic assay is an objective measure and the separation is documented, but no limit of quantification, precision or accuracy is printed, while statements about when drug and metabolite had disappeared rest on an unstated detection limit.

No protocol; no test statistics or p values for the stated null comparisons across seventy tabulated values; two preliminary sub-studies reported only in the Discussion, one of them in a single volunteer; and the integration window for the norketamine area differs between the abstract (to 6 hours for the nasal spray) and Table 2 (to 8 hours for every preparation).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The within-person design and the stereoselective assay are appropriate for the question, and every man received every preparation, which removes between-person variation from the comparison. The overall judgment is set by the open, unrandomized order, by two conditions that did not deliver what their labels say (sublingual tablets swallowed with saliva, suppositories given without a standard bowel preparation), and by reporting that gives no test statistics, no intervals and no individual values for a sample of three. The source can be cited for the plasma concentration-time profiles of ketamine and norketamine enantiomers after these five preparations in three healthy men, and for bioavailability figures of roughly 18%, 32%, 29-31% and 44-46% with the sample size of three attached and with the sublingual caveat; it cannot be cited for any analgesic or clinical effect, for equivalence between preparations or enantiomers, for a half-life by any route other than intravenous, or for figures applicable to patients.

key_findings.finding: After a 20 mg intravenous injection, plasma ketamine fell biexponentially with a terminal half-life of 126.8 minutes (SD 47.4) for the (R)- and 117.3 minutes (SD 47.9) for the (S)-enantiomer; total clearance was 1.1 and 1.2 L/h/kg and the steady-state volume of distribution 2.5 L/kg for both.

Bioavailability relative to the intravenous injection was 18.3% (SD 4.7) and 17.6% (SD 3.8) for the tablet, 32.2% (SD 8.2) and 32.1% (SD 7.2) for the sublingual tablet, 28.9% (SD 18.9) and 30.8% (SD 30.6) for the suppository, and 43.8% (SD 11.4) and 46.4% (SD 12.9) for the nasal spray, for the (R)- and (S)-enantiomers respectively; the nasal spray gave the highest value of the preparations tested.
key_findings.note: Each figure is a mean of three men, and for the suppository the standard deviation is about the size of the mean. Editors' calculation: recomputing each figure from the tabulated mean areas instead of as a mean of individual ratios reproduces every preparation within 3 percentage points (tablet 21.0 and 20.6, sublingual 31.5 and 35.0, suppository 29.7 and 27.8, nasal 44.5 and 46.0), so the table is internally consistent; the tablet is the only preparation for which the recomputation is higher for both enantiomers. Individual values are not printed, so the printed means of ratios cannot be reproduced exactly.

key_findings.finding: Peak concentrations after the four non-injected preparations were between 29 and 62 ng/mL for both enantiomers, reached at about 17-40 minutes, with the sublingual tablet giving the highest peak (61.6 and 56.9 ng/mL) and the nasal spray the lowest (29.4 and 29.3 ng/mL) at half the nominal amount.
key_findings.note: The tablet, sublingual tablet and suppository conditions each contained 50 mg and the nasal spray 25 mg, so peaks are not comparable across preparations without that difference.

key_findings.finding: Norketamine exposure differed sharply between preparations: the area to 8 hours was 533.8 and 494.9 ng*h/mL after the tablet, 462.9 and 408.7 after the sublingual tablet, 322.6 and 282.6 after the suppository, 173.8 and 149.8 after the injection, and 115.9 and 100.7 after the nasal spray, for the (R)- and (S)-enantiomers.

The ratio of the norketamine area to the ketamine area was highest after the swallowed tablet, which the authors describe as about eight times, and lowest after the nasal spray, where the two areas were similar; they read this as showing that the tablet is subject to extensive first-pass metabolism and the nasal spray largely escapes it.
key_findings.locator: Results, last (4th) paragraph (begins p. 39); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 42, continues to p. 43); values in Tables 1 and 2 (pp. 41-42)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Tables 1 and 2: the ratios are 7.4 and 7.6 after the tablet, 4.3 and 3.7 after the sublingual tablet, 3.2 and 3.2 after the suppository and 1.5 and 1.4 after the nasal spray, so 'about eight times' rounds up from about seven and a half.

key_findings.finding: No pharmacokinetic parameter of ketamine or norketamine differed significantly between the (R)- and (S)-enantiomers, or between the five preparations, by analysis of variance.
key_findings.locator: Results, last (4th) paragraph, which begins on p. 39 and ends at the top of the left column of p. 40
key_findings.note: A null result in three people with no test statistic, degrees of freedom or p value printed anywhere; it cannot be read as evidence that the preparations or enantiomers behave alike.

key_findings.finding: Ketamine was detectable 5-20 minutes after the tablet, sublingual tablet, suppository and nasal spray, with mean peaks of 30-50 ng/mL at 20-30 minutes, and had fallen below the detection limit by 4-6 hours; norketamine appeared 10-30 minutes after every route, with mean peaks at 30 minutes to 1.5 hours.
key_findings.note: The detection limit on which these statements depend is never given in the paper.

key_findings.finding: The sublingual tablets were swallowed using saliva, so part of the sublingual condition was gastrointestinal absorption; in a preliminary comparison the one-hour area and peak concentration were 35-50% lower when saliva was not swallowed for an hour.
key_findings.note: The number of participants and the data for this preliminary comparison are not reported, and the figure of about 32% for sublingual bioavailability therefore describes a mixed sublingual and oral route.

key_findings.finding: The authors attribute the large variation in the rectal values to the degree of absorption differing between participants, because not all of them had a rectal enema before the suppository was inserted.

In a preliminary study in one volunteer the area after the nasal spray increased almost linearly between the two amounts tested; the authors nevertheless state that the amount of ketamine delivered by the atomizer is difficult to control.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 42, continues to p. 43)

key_findings.finding: No elimination half-life is reported for the tablet, sublingual tablet, suppository or nasal spray; the half-life column of Table 1 is filled only for the intravenous injection.
key_findings.note: A claim about how long ketamine persists after any of these preparations cannot be anchored to this paper.

key_findings.finding: The Introduction places this study's figures beside earlier ones: swallowed ketamine at 0.5 mg/kg is reported to have had a bioavailability of approximately 17% in an earlier study, and nasal and rectal bioavailability for the induction of anaesthesia in children (3 to 9 mg/kg) to have been reported as approximately 50% and 25%.
key_findings.note: These are the paper's own second-hand comparisons, not measurements made here; the earlier oral figure is the one Clements et al. (1982) printed as 16.6% (card sc_clements_1982).

key_findings.finding: Table 1 prints a total clearance and a steady-state volume of distribution only for the 20 mg injection; neither is given for the tablet, sublingual tablet, suppository or nasal spray.
key_findings.note: With the half-life column likewise filled only for the injection, the paper supports statements about how much of each preparation reaches the blood, not about how fast the body clears it.

key_findings.finding: The three men weighed 60 to 72 kg and every preparation was given as a fixed amount (50 mg, or 25 mg for the nasal spray) rather than per kilogram of body weight, so the amount delivered per kilogram varied by about a fifth across the sample.
key_findings.locator: Methods, subjects paragraph and Drug administration paragraph
key_findings.note: No individual values are printed, so this variation cannot be seen in the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The times to peak for the nasal spray, 22.5 minutes (SD 9.6) for the (R)- and 17.5 (SD 5.0) for the (S)-enantiomer, cannot be means of three observations taken at the stated sampling times, which are all multiples of 5 minutes: the sum of three such times is a multiple of 5, so their mean cannot be 22.5 or 17.5. Editors' calculation: both means and both standard deviations are reproduced exactly by four observations (10, 20, 30 and 30 minutes gives 22.5 with SD 9.6; 10, 20, 20 and 20 gives 17.5 with SD 5.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the nasal row rests on more than three determinations, or sampling times other than those listed were used; in either case the stated sample size of three does not describe the nasal row, which is the row the later review cites for nasal bioavailability.

reporting_issues.issue: The time to peak for the tablet (S)-ketamine, 30.0 minutes (SD 30.0), is reproduced by only one set of three values from the stated sampling grid, namely 0, 30 and 60 minutes (editors' calculation), and 0 minutes is the pre-dose blank, which cannot be a time to peak.
reporting_issues.consequence: That cell is not consistent with the sampling schedule as described; the tablet's time to peak should not be quoted from it.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the norketamine area after the nasal spray as the area to 6 hours, while Table 2 heads every column as the area to 8 hours; the Results state that norketamine was below the detection limit 8 hours after the spray.
reporting_issues.consequence: The nasal row is integrated over a different window from the other four, so the norketamine areas in Table 2 are not directly comparable across preparations, and the comparison the Discussion draws between them is to that extent not like with like.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the norketamine area after the sublingual tablet and the suppository as 280-460 ng*h/mL, but the highest value in that set in Table 2 is 462.9 (sublingual, (R)-norketamine).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the abstract's range should not be quoted as the measured range.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that the norketamine area after the tablet was about eight times the ketamine area; the printed values give 7.4 and 7.6 (editors' calculation from Tables 1 and 2: 533.8 divided by 72.3 and 494.9 divided by 64.9).
reporting_issues.consequence: A small rounding upward, but the ratio is one of the paper's main arguments for first-pass metabolism and should be quoted from the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: No limit of quantification or detection limit is stated anywhere, although the Results use the phrase 'less than the detection limit' three times as the basis for statements about when ketamine and norketamine had disappeared.
reporting_issues.consequence: Statements about the disappearance of drug and metabolite, and the choice of integration window for the nasal row, cannot be checked or compared with other studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The ethics committee is named after one form of the hospital's name in the Methods and another in the affiliations.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial; recorded only because the approving body should be identifiable.
